241: C is correct because an Amazon RDS cross-Region read replica keeps a continuously replicated copy of the PostgreSQL data in a second Region, so the data remains available and online in multiple Regions at all times, and RDS manages the replication with minimal operational overhead. Multi-AZ only provides high availability within a single Region, copied snapshots are point-in-time backups rather than an online database, and running PostgreSQL on EC2 requires the company to manage the cluster itself.
242: C is correct because a multivalue answer routing policy in Amazon Route 53 returns multiple IP addresses in response to each DNS query and works with health checks, so only the IP addresses of healthy EC2 instances are returned to clients. A simple routing policy returns all configured values but cannot filter out unhealthy instances, making it unsuitable for this requirement.
243: A is correct because an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway caches Amazon S3 data on premises and presents it as a native NFS or SMB file share, giving the clinics' file-based on-premises applications low-latency access while S3 remains the durable backing store. A volume gateway exposes iSCSI block volumes rather than file access, DataSync is a migration tool rather than an ongoing access solution, and EFS cannot be attached directly to on-premises servers.
244: C is correct because moving the database to Amazon Aurora with a read replica in another Availability Zone makes the data tier highly available, and creating an AMI used by an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer makes the web tier highly available and able to scale with user demand. The other options either keep manually launched instances in a single Availability Zone, which is a single point of failure with no automatic scaling, or leave the database on EC2 where the company must manage its availability and backups itself.
245: D is correct because lowering the maximum size of the development environment's Auto Scaling group caps the number of EC2 instances that can run and directly reduces cost, while leaving the production environment untouched so it can still handle its high-traffic periods. Reducing the target group to a single instance would break the requirement of at least two targets, least outstanding requests only changes traffic distribution, and shrinking instance sizes in both environments would degrade production performance.
246: D is correct because an internet-facing Application Load Balancer must be associated with public subnets, one per Availability Zone, so that internet traffic can reach the load balancer, while the EC2 instances can safely remain in the private subnets and receive traffic from the ALB. The original architecture fails because the ALB was not reachable from the internet, and the alternatives of moving instances to public subnets or routing private subnets directly to an internet gateway would unnecessarily expose the instances instead of fixing the load balancer placement.
247: C is correct because long-running transactions on the source DB instance must be allowed to complete before replica creation, since the binary log coordinates used for replication can only advance after open transactions finish, and an active long transaction can stall the process. E is correct because enabling automatic backups by setting the retention period to a nonzero value is a prerequisite for RDS MySQL read replicas, as RDS uses the resulting binary logs to replicate to the replica. RDS enables binlog replication automatically once backups are turned on, so it is not a separate manual action.
248: D is correct because routing incoming requests to an Amazon SQS queue durably buffers every submitted job so no data is lost when instances are busy, and an EC2 Auto Scaling group that scales on queue depth automatically adds processing capacity as user load grows. Putting copies behind an ALB adds no extra processing capability, resizing instances vertically does not scale with load, and the reported bottleneck is CPU rather than S3 throughput, so a VPC endpoint would not help.
249: D is correct because Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed native Windows file system that provides SMB access out of the box, so application servers can connect without the company operating any file server infrastructure. The Storage Gateway options are hybrid caching services for on-premises workloads rather than managed shared storage in AWS, and hosting a file share on an EC2 instance is a self-managed solution.
250: D is correct because publishing VPC Flow Logs to Amazon S3 and applying an S3 Lifecycle policy that transitions objects to S3 Standard-IA after 90 days keeps the logs in Standard class while they are frequently accessed and then lowers storage costs for the intermittent access period while the logs remain available. A CloudWatch Logs expiration of 90 days would delete the logs rather than retain them, Kinesis is a streaming service rather than a cost-effective archive, and CloudTrail is designed for API audit records, not VPC Flow Logs.
251: B is correct because a NAT gateway placed in a public subnet lets the EC2 instance in the private subnet initiate outbound connections, such as downloading monthly security updates, while the instance itself remains unreachable from the internet. Pointing the private subnet route table at an internet gateway would not work because the instance has no public IP address, and a NAT instance placed in the same private subnet would itself have no path to the internet.
252: A is correct because Amazon EFS is a fully managed, elastic NFS file system that can be mounted simultaneously by multiple EC2 instances, grows automatically as files are added over time, and stores data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones for built-in redundancy. EBS volumes can only be attached to a single instance in normal use, S3 Glacier Deep Archive is an archival storage class with long retrieval times and no shared file-system interface, and AWS Backup manages backups rather than providing live shared storage.
253: C is correct because IAM grants the union of permissions from all policies attached to the group, and those combined policies include permission to terminate, that is delete, Amazon EC2 instances, so the cloud engineer can perform that action. Deleting IAM users, directories, or CloudWatch Logs is not granted by the attached policies, so those actions are denied.
254: B is correct because using the security group ID of another tier as the source or destination in a security group rule restricts traffic to exactly the instances belonging to that tier, which enforces the principle of least privilege and automatically stays current as instances are added or removed by Auto Scaling. Instance IDs cannot be used in security group rules, and VPC or subnet CIDR ranges permit traffic from any resource in that range, which is broader than necessary.
255: D is correct because an Amazon SQS FIFO queue provides exactly-once processing and deduplicates messages, so the payment service retrieves each order message a single time, processes it, and deletes it from the queue, which prevents duplicate orders when users resubmit the checkout form. Kinesis Data Firehose is a one-way streaming delivery service, CloudTrail records AWS API calls rather than application requests, and Amazon SNS is publish-subscribe messaging without the exactly-once processing guarantee needed here.
256: B is correct because enabling versioning on the S3 bucket preserves every version of the documents, so users can download, modify, and upload while all prior versions remain available for recovery, and deletions only create delete markers rather than destroying data. D is correct because enabling MFA Delete requires MFA authentication to permanently delete object versions or alter the versioning configuration, which prevents accidental or unauthorized permanent deletion of documents. The other options address ACLs, IAM permissions, or encryption but do not provide version history or deletion protection.
257: A is correct because a CloudWatch metric stream continuously streams Auto Scaling metrics in near real time to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose, which delivers them to Amazon S3 in a fully serverless pipeline that runs completely independently of the EC2 instance launch process. A Lambda function on a schedule polls on an interval and is not near real time, and a bootstrap script or EMR cluster would add overhead to instance launches or require managing additional infrastructure.
258: D is correct because an AWS Glue ETL job is a fully managed, Spark-based service purpose-built for large-scale data format conversions, and triggering it with a Lambda function on each S3 PUT event makes the pipeline event driven with no servers to manage. A Lambda function alone is poorly suited to converting 1 GB files because of its 15-minute timeout and memory limits, and scheduled Athena queries or a self-managed Spark cluster add more moving parts and operational overhead than a Glue job invoked directly on upload.
259: A is correct because AWS Backup provides a centralized backup plan with a daily schedule and a lifecycle rule that retains recovery points for 2 years, and it creates consistent, automated, restorable backups of RDS DB instances across the account. Amazon DLM only manages EBS snapshots rather than RDS backups, transaction logs shipped to CloudWatch Logs are not restorable backups, and AWS DMS with CDC streams ongoing changes rather than producing consistent daily backups.
260: D is correct because joining the FSx for Windows File Server file system to the self-managed on-premises Active Directory allows the existing AD users and groups to continue enforcing access to the SMB shares, folders, and files through native Windows ACLs after the move to AWS. IAM groups, tags, and service-linked roles do not control file-level access on an SMB file system, so Active Directory integration is the required mechanism.
